notes:
Sub-atomic particles

  • Electron: charge $-1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, mass $9.1\times10^{-31}$ kg (discovered by Thomson, cathode rays). Proton (Goldstein) and neutron (Chadwick) reside in the nucleus.
  • Atomic number $Z$ = number of protons; mass number $A = Z + n$. Isotopes: same $Z$, different $A$ (e.g. $^{12}$C, $^{14}$C). Isobars: same $A$, different $Z$. Isotones: same number of neutrons.

Atomic models

  • Rutherford's α-scattering: most α-particles passed straight through (mostly empty space); a few deflected sharply (small, dense, positive nucleus). Could not explain atomic stability (accelerating electron should radiate energy and spiral into nucleus).
  • Bohr's model: electrons revolve in fixed circular orbits (stationary states) with quantised angular momentum $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$. Energy is emitted/absorbed only when an electron jumps orbits: $\Delta E = h\nu$.

Bohr model formulas (H-like species)

Radius$r_n = 0.529\dfrac{n^2}{Z}\,\text{Å}$
Energy$E_n = -13.6\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}\,\text{eV}$
Velocity$v_n = 2.18\times10^6\dfrac{Z}{n}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$

Rydberg formula: $\dfrac1\lambda = R Z^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2}-\dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$, $R = 1.097\times10^7\,\text{m}^{-1}$. Lyman ($n_1=1$, UV), Balmer ($n_1=2$, visible), Paschen ($n_1=3$, IR) series.

Dual nature & uncertainty

  • de Broglie: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{h}{p}$ — matter shows wave nature.
  • Heisenberg uncertainty: $\Delta x\cdot\Delta p \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$ — cannot simultaneously know exact position and momentum; makes fixed Bohr orbits invalid, replaced by orbitals (regions of probability).

Quantum numbers & filling rules

  • $n$ (shell, energy), $l$ (subshell/shape, $0$ to $n-1$; s,p,d,f), $m_l$ (orientation, $-l$ to $+l$), $m_s$ (spin, $\pm\tfrac12$).
  • Aufbau: fill in order of increasing $(n+l)$; for equal $(n+l)$, lower $n$ first. Pauli exclusion: no two electrons in an atom have identical 4 quantum numbers (max $2n^2$ per shell, $2(2l+1)$ per subshell). Hund's rule: degenerate orbitals singly filled first with parallel spins (max multiplicity), giving extra stability to fully-filled and half-filled configurations (e.g. Cr: [Ar]3d$^5$4s$^1$, Cu: [Ar]3d$^{10}$4s$^1$).

Exam tip

2–3 questions every year: a Bohr-model numerical (radius/energy/wavelength ratio for H or He$^+$), electronic configuration exceptions (Cr, Cu), and one on quantum numbers or de Broglie/uncertainty. Memorise $R_H$, $13.6$ eV, and the $2n^2$ rule.

questions.q: The number of electrons, protons and neutrons in $^{35}_{17}$Cl are respectively
questions.explanation: $Z = 17$ gives protons = electrons = 17; neutrons $= A - Z = 35 - 17 = 18$.

questions.q: According to Bohr's postulate, the angular momentum of an electron in the $n$th orbit is
questions.explanation: Bohr's quantisation condition: $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, $n = 1, 2, 3\dots$

The energy of an electron in the second Bohr orbit of hydrogen is
The wavelength associated with an electron moving with velocity $v$ is $\lambda$. If the velocity is doubled, the new wavelength is
questions.explanation: de Broglie: $\lambda = h/(mv)$, so $\lambda \propto 1/v$; doubling $v$ halves $\lambda$.

questions.q: Which set of quantum numbers is not possible?
questions.explanation: $l$ can only range from $0$ to $n-1$. For $n=2$, $l$ can be 0 or 1, not 2.

questions.q: The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the M shell ($n=3$) is
questions.explanation: Maximum electrons per shell $= 2n^2 = 2\times9 = 18$.

questions.q: The electronic configuration of Cr (Z = 24) is best represented as
questions.explanation: A half-filled 3d$^5$ and filled 4s$^1$ configuration is more stable than 3d$^4$4s$^2$, due to extra exchange stabilisation.

questions.q: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states that
options: energy of an electron is quantised
electrons move in fixed circular orbits
position and momentum of a small particle cannot both be measured exactly and simultaneously
an atom's orbitals are always spherical
questions.explanation: $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \ge h/4\pi$; the principle is significant for microscopic particles like electrons, not macroscopic bodies.

questions.q: In the hydrogen spectrum, the Balmer series arises from transitions to
questions.explanation: Balmer series corresponds to electronic transitions ending at $n_1 = 2$, lying in the visible region.

questions.q: Rutherford's α-particle scattering experiment led to the conclusion that
options: the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus
questions.explanation: Large-angle scattering of a few α-particles indicated a small volume of concentrated positive charge and mass — the nucleus.

questions.q: The number of orbitals possible for $n = 3$ is
questions.explanation: Total orbitals per shell $= n^2 = 9$ (1 for $l=0$, 3 for $l=1$, 5 for $l=2$).

questions.q: According to Hund's rule, electrons in degenerate orbitals are filled such that
options: they pair up as fast as possible
they occupy separate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing
the orbital with lowest $m_l$ fills first
questions.explanation: Maximum spin multiplicity gives lower energy (exchange stabilisation), so singly occupied degenerate orbitals are preferred first.

questions.q: The wavelength of the photon emitted when an electron in a hydrogen atom jumps from $n=3$ to $n=1$ is (given $R_H = 1.097\times10^7\,\text{m}^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1\lambda = R_H\left(1 - \dfrac19\right) = 1.097\times10^7\times\dfrac89 = 9.75\times10^6\,\text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda \approx 102.6$ nm.

questions.q: Isotopes of an element have the same
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons (atomic number $Z$) but differ in the number of neutrons and hence mass number.

questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through a potential difference $V$ is proportional to
questions.explanation: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}$, so $\lambda \propto 1/\sqrt{V}$.

questions.q: Which subshell is filled immediately after 4s according to the Aufbau principle?
questions.explanation: Using $(n+l)$ values, 3d ($n+l=5$) has lower energy than 4p ($n+l=5$ but higher $n$) is filled right after 4s in the Aufbau order 1s,2s,2p,3s,3p,4s,3d...

questions.q: The total number of s, p and d electrons in Fe (Z = 26, [Ar]3d$^6$4s$^2$) are respectively
questions.explanation: Full configuration: 1s$^2$2s$^2$2p$^6$3s$^2$3p$^6$3d$^6$4s$^2$. s-electrons: 1s,2s,3s,4s = $4\times2=8$; p-electrons: 2p,3p = $2\times6=12$; d-electrons: 3d = 6. Total $8+12+6=26$.

questions.q: The minimum uncertainty in the velocity of an electron confined to a region of size $\Delta x$ is proportional to
questions.explanation: From $\Delta x\cdot\Delta v \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi m}$, $\Delta v \propto 1/\Delta x$ for fixed mass.

questions.q: An orbital with $n = 4, l = 2$ is designated as
questions.explanation: $l = 0,1,2,3$ correspond to s, p, d, f respectively; so $l=2$ with $n=4$ is 4d.

questions.q: The threshold frequency in the photoelectric effect is
options: the frequency below which electrons are always emitted
the minimum frequency of light needed to eject an electron from a metal surface
the frequency of incident light having maximum energy
the frequency at which a metal melts
questions.explanation: Below the threshold frequency $\nu_0$, no photoelectrons are emitted regardless of intensity; above it, kinetic energy of ejected electrons increases with frequency.

questions.q: The energy of a photon of wavelength 400 nm is (h = $6.626\times10^{-34}$ J s, c = $3\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $E = hc/\lambda = (6.626\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^8)/(400\times10^{-9}) \approx 4.97\times10^{-19}$ J.

questions.q: The number of radial nodes in a 3p orbital is
questions.explanation: Radial nodes $= n - l - 1 = 3 - 1 - 1 = 1$.

questions.q: The number of angular nodes in a d orbital is
questions.explanation: Angular nodes $= l = 2$ for a d orbital ($l=2$).

questions.q: The total number of nodes in a 4s orbital is
questions.explanation: Total nodes $= n - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3$ (all radial, since $l=0$).

questions.q: The series limit (shortest wavelength) of the Lyman series is
questions.explanation: Series limit corresponds to $n_2 \to \infty$: $1/\lambda = R_H(1/1^2 - 0) = 1.097\times10^7$, so $\lambda = 1/(1.097\times10^7) \approx 91.2$ nm.

questions.q: Which of the following electronic configurations is NOT possible, as it violates the Pauli exclusion principle?
questions.explanation: A p subshell can hold a maximum of 6 electrons (3 orbitals × 2); 2p$^7$ would require two electrons with identical quantum numbers, violating Pauli's exclusion principle.

questions.q: A subshell with azimuthal quantum number $l = 3$ is designated as
questions.explanation: $l = 0,1,2,3$ correspond to s, p, d, f subshells respectively.

questions.q: In the ground state of nitrogen (Z = 7, 1s$^2$2s$^2$2p$^3$), the number of electrons with $m_l = 0$ is
questions.explanation: 1s ($m_l=0$): 2 electrons; 2s ($m_l=0$): 2 electrons; 2p$^3$ singly occupies $m_l = -1, 0, +1$ by Hund's rule, contributing 1 electron with $m_l=0$. Total $= 2+2+1 = 5$.

questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V is (using $\lambda(\text{Å}) = 12.27/\sqrt{V}$)
Which of the following could NOT be explained by Bohr's model of the atom?
options: the splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect)
questions.explanation: Bohr's model successfully explained the hydrogen spectrum and energy quantisation but failed to account for the Zeeman and Stark effects and spectra of multi-electron atoms.

questions.q: The energy required to excite an electron in a hydrogen atom from $n=1$ to $n=2$ is
The ionisation energy of He$^+$ ion (Z = 2) is
questions.explanation: Ionisation energy $= 13.6\,Z^2/n^2 = 13.6\times4/1 = 54.4$ eV, since removing the electron from $n=1$ needs $-E_1$.

questions.q: Among proton, electron, neutron and alpha particle, the one with negligible mass compared to the others is the
questions.explanation: The electron's mass ($9.1\times10^{-31}$ kg) is about 1836 times smaller than a proton's, and is often neglected in mass number calculations.

questions.q: Which pair of nuclides represents isobars?
questions.explanation: Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers; $^{40}$Ar (Z=18) and $^{40}$Ca (Z=20) both have mass number 40.

questions.q: The frequency of a photon having energy $3.03\times10^{-19}$ J is (h = $6.626\times10^{-34}$ J s)
The shape of an orbital is determined by which quantum number?
questions.explanation: The azimuthal (angular momentum) quantum number $l$ decides the subshell type and hence the shape of the orbital (s, p, d, f).

questions.q: The maximum number of electrons that a subshell with $l = 2$ can accommodate is
questions.explanation: Maximum electrons in a subshell $= 2(2l+1) = 2(5) = 10$ for a d subshell ($l=2$).

questions.q: The wavelength of the second line of the Balmer series ($n_1=2$ to $n_2=4$) is closest to
questions.explanation: $1/\lambda = R_H(1/4 - 1/16) = 1.097\times10^7\times0.1875 \approx 2.057\times10^6\,\text{m}^{-1}$, giving $\lambda \approx 486$ nm (the H$_\beta$ line).

questions.q: Which of the following statements about orbitals is correct?
options: An orbital and an orbit refer to the same concept
An orbital can hold a maximum of two electrons, and they must have opposite spins
An orbital can hold up to three electrons if their spins are parallel
questions.explanation: By the Pauli exclusion principle, an orbital holds at most two electrons, and if both are present their spins must be paired (opposite).
